title: Produce Grading and Sorting
summary: Grade fruit, vegetable and grain lots from camera images at collection centres and packhouses, with defect breakdowns and photo evidence that buyers, FPOs and farmers can all check.

seo.title: AI Produce Grading and Sorting | VipraTech
seo.description: Computer vision that grades produce and grain samples by size, colour and defects at FPO collection centres and packhouses, with photo evidence per lot.
keywords: fruit and vegetable sorting computer vision

problem.intro: At a collection centre or packhouse, grading decides what the farmer is paid and what the buyer accepts. It is often done by eye on a sample, by a grader who may be tired by the afternoon, and disputes over grade are settled by argument rather than evidence.

pain_points.title: Inconsistent manual grading
pain_points.detail: Two graders can place the same lot of tomatoes or pomegranates in different grades, and the same grader drifts over a long shift.

pain_points.title: Disputes with farmers and buyers
pain_points.detail: When a farmer questions a deduction or a buyer rejects a consignment, there is no record of what the lot actually looked like.

pain_points.title: Slow sample analysis for grain
pain_points.detail: Counting broken, shrivelled, discoloured and foreign-matter grains in a wheat or chana sample by hand takes time at peak arrivals.

pain_points.title: Grade specs that vary by buyer
pain_points.detail: Exporters, modern retail and processors each set their own size, colour and defect limits, which graders must remember.

solution.overview: We build a vision-based grading station for sample trays or conveyor lines. A fixed camera under controlled lighting captures each sample or piece, and models measure size, shape, colour and surface defects such as bruises, cracks, rot and pest damage. For grain, the system counts and classifies kernels on a tray image, including broken, damaged and foreign matter. Grade rules are configured per commodity and buyer specification. Each lot gets a grade, a defect breakdown and stored images, linked to the farmer and weighbridge record. Borderline lots and disputes go to a QC assayer, who views the same images and can override the grade with a reason.
capabilities: Size, shape and colour measurement for fruit and vegetables
Surface defect detection for bruising, cracks, rot and pest damage
Kernel-level grain sample analysis for broken, damaged and foreign matter
Configurable grade rules per commodity and buyer specification
Lot-level grade record with stored images
QC override with mandatory reason capture

workflow.title: Capture the sample
workflow.detail: The operator places a sample on the tray or lets produce pass the conveyor camera, and scans the lot or farmer token.

workflow.title: Measure and detect defects
workflow.detail: Models measure each item or kernel and mark visible defects and foreign matter.

workflow.title: Apply grade rules
workflow.detail: Measurements are compared with the commodity and buyer specification to produce a grade and defect breakdown.

workflow.title: Check borderline lots
workflow.detail: Lots near a grade boundary, or with poor image quality, are flagged instead of being auto-graded.

workflow.title: QC assayer review
workflow.detail: The assayer reviews flagged lots and any farmer or buyer dispute using the stored images, and confirms or overrides the grade.

workflow.title: Publish the result
workflow.detail: The grade and images are attached to the lot in the procurement system and shared with the farmer and buyer.

inputs: Sample tray or conveyor images per lot
Lot or farmer token and weighbridge record
Commodity grade specifications from buyers, or AGMARK standards where used
Reference images of each grade and defect, labelled by your QC team
outputs: Grade per lot with defect breakdown
Stored images linked to each lot
Borderline and dispute queue for QC
Grade history by farmer, village and season
human_in_the_loop: QC assayers review every borderline lot and every dispute raised by a farmer or buyer, using the same stored images. Overrides require a reason, which is used to recalibrate grade rules and models.
integrations: WhatsApp Business API or SMS gateway for farmer receipts
guardrails: Lighting and camera calibration check at the start of each shift
All grade overrides logged with user and reason
Periodic blind re-grading of sampled lots by QC staff
Separate model versions per commodity, released only after QC sign-off
compliance_notes: Where produce is graded under AGMARK, grade rules can be configured to the published grade standards, with the authorised grader keeping final responsibility.
Images and farmer identifiers are stored with access controls and retention periods agreed with you.

pilot.scope: One commodity at one collection centre or packhouse line, run in parallel with manual grading on the same lots.
deliverables: Labelled reference set agreed with your QC team
Working grading station for one commodity
Plan for further commodities and sites

what_we_measure.how: Model grade compared with the QC assayer's grade on the same lots.
Defects marked by the model checked against a QC-labelled sample.
Grading time per lot measured with and without the station during peak arrivals.
Count of farmer or buyer disputes where stored images were used to settle the grade.

faqs.a: A good industrial camera, or a high-end phone camera, in a simple lighting enclosure is usually enough for sample-tray grading. Conveyor lines need a fixed camera and a trigger. We specify the setup for your commodity during the pilot.

faqs.q: Can it handle different buyers' grade specs?
faqs.a: Yes. Grade rules are configured per commodity and buyer, so the same images can be graded against an exporter's spec and a processor's spec. Your QC team approves every rule set.

faqs.q: What about internal defects we cannot see?
faqs.a: Camera-based grading sees surface and shape only. Internal browning, hollow heart or insect damage inside the grain need other methods, and we say so clearly in the scope.

faqs.q: Will farmers trust a machine grade?
faqs.a: Trust usually comes from transparency. Each farmer can be shown the images and defect marks for their lot, and disputes go to a human assayer who can override the grade.
